Apparatus criticus

  • Text of Ferrua following the transcription of Amico, but supplying extensive restorations;
  • lines.1-2: [ἐνθάδε κατάκεινται | [ἡ μακαρία]ς μνήμης Ferrua; [ἐνθάδε κεῖται | ὁ τῆς μακαρία]ς μνήμης CIG IV 9498; ὁ τῆς μακαρία]ς μνήμης IG XIV 555
  • line.4: [ἐλθοῦσα κ(αὶ) Ἰο]ῦστος πιστός Ferrua; φιλόχρι]στος CIG IV 9498
  • lines.5-6: [ἠγόρασαν] παρὰ Ἀλε|[ξάνδρου Ferrua; πολυπόθητος] παρὰ ἀε|[λφῶν CIG IV 9498; ἠγόρασα τὸν τόπον] παρὰ Ἀλε|[ξάνδρου IG XIV 555
  • line.6: εὐ]μοιρείτων Ferrua; ΜΟΙΡΕΙΠΩΝ Amico; τῶν εὐμοιρειτῶν IG XIV 555

English translation

Marta Fogagnolo

Here lie …, of blessed memory, … having come to the end of a virtuous life, and the faithful Iustus, who purchased (the tomb) from Alexander. May they rest in peace. May they fare well.

commentary

The funerary inscription most likely originally opened with the formula ἐνθάδε κεῖται (l. 1). According to Ferrua’s restoration, the epitaph commemorated two deceased individuals: a woman, identified by the expression ἡ μακαρίας μνήμης followed by her personal name (for this formula, characteristic of Christian funerary inscriptions and corresponding to the Latin bonae memoriae, see IG XIV 537 (ISic001356) from Catania; cf. Agnello 1953, 59), and a man named Ἰοῦστος (cf. SEG 26.1173 from Catania). Lines 5–6 probably contained a record of the purchase of the burial plot or funerary monument by the deceased themselves during their lifetime from a certain Alexander. The final invocation, εὐμοιρείτων, may be addressed to the deceased and echo similar invocations in the second-person singular (εὐμοίρει: IG XIV 114, IG XIV 124, SEG 45.1419.5, all from Syracuse).

bibliography

  • Amico 1741 272 no.XVII https://biblio.inscriptiones.org/epig10002186
  • Kirchhoff 1877 9498 https://biblio.inscriptiones.org/epig10001249
  • Kaibel 1890 555 https://biblio.inscriptiones.org/epig10001072
  • Ferrua 1989 117 no.447 https://biblio.inscriptiones.org/epig10001995
  • Agnello 1953 59 https://biblio.inscriptiones.org/epig10002211

Amico records lunate sigma and uncial omega, but quadrate epsilon (but epsilon appears always to be printed quadrate in this work).
